Date-override check allows slots that only partially overlap the override

The condition marks a slot as outside an override only when slotEndTime is before or the same as the override start, or slotStartTime is after the override end. A slot that starts before the override and ends inside it, starts inside and ends after it, or starts exactly at the override end is treated as inside the override and allowed. Since fixed-host slots are generated from aggregate availability, this lets a round-robin event be booked while the fixed host is unavailable.

Fixed host with no working hours on a day is treated as available

This `workingHours.find(...)` only rejects a slot when a working-hour entry for the day exists and the slot start is outside that entry. If no entry has `days` including `slotStartTime.day()`, `find` returns undefined and execution continues to the busy check, which can return true. For a round-robin slot generated by another host on a day the fixed host does not work, this makes the fixed host appear available and allows a booking outside their schedule.

Multiple same-day date overrides are not all considered

`dateOverrides.find` returns true as soon as one matching-day override is outside the slot, causing `checkIfIsAvailable` to return false immediately. Later same-day overrides that do contain the slot are never checked. If a fixed host has several overrides on one day, for example 10-11 and 14-15, a slot inside the later override can be blocked because the first override did not encompass it.

Round-robin fixed-host date override scenario is not tested

The PR title/description says date overrides of fixed hosts should be taken into account for round-robin events, but the added test only covers a personal event date override with a different invitee timezone. The new `checkIfIsAvailable` date-override and working-hours paths for fixed hosts are the most complex part of this change and have no regression test.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError when installation metadata lacks sender

The user mismatch check dereferences integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] unconditionally. Integrations created by build_integration without state["sender"] (or existing rows from before sender was recorded) will have no "sender" key in metadata. On the reinstallation path where the Integration exists but no OrganizationIntegration exists, this raises KeyError and returns a 500/Internal Error instead of the GitHub integration failure page. Use integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login") and fail closed if it is missing.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

false_positives.candidate:
GitHub user validation skipped when Integration does not exist yet

In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, when Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id) raises DoesNotExist, the code returns pipeline.next_step() before comparing pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") to the installation's sender. For a first-time installation (or if the installation webhook has not yet created the Integration row), pipeline.next_step() proceeds to build_integration and creates the integration without any sender-vs-OAuth-user check. An attacker who can reach the setup URL with a valid installation_id and complete OAuth as a different GitHub user can attach that installation to their Sentry organization. The check should not be conditional on the Integration row already existing; the sender must be obtained elsewhere or installation should fail closed.

get_user_info exceptions escape OAuthLoginView

The token-response parsing around safe_urlread is wrapped in try/except, but get_user_info(payload["access_token"]) is not. get_user_info makes an HTTP request to GitHub and can raise on network failures, timeouts, non-JSON bodies, or HTTP errors that it does not convert to a plain missing-login dict. Because dispatch does not catch these exceptions, a valid pipeline can return a 500 instead of rendering the installation failure page. Wrap get_user_info in an error-handling block and return error(request, self.active_organization) when the user cannot be fetched.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
queued timestamp is evaluated once at import time

In a dataclass, default values are evaluated when the class is defined, not per instance. `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` stamps every `AssignmentSource` created without an explicit `queued` with the module import time. `from_integration` does not pass `queued`, so all sources created via inbound sync share a stale creation/queue timestamp; any future use for ordering, TTL, or queue delay will be wrong. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` after importing `field`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.
to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.

false_positives.candidate:
Outbound task always passes new arguments to overridable integration methods

The task now calls `installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source)` and later `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(..., assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source)`, even when no source exists (the argument is `None`). The base `should_sync` signature was updated, but concrete integration subclasses that override the old one-argument `should_sync` or define `sync_assignee_outbound` without `assignment_source`/`**kwargs` were valid before and will now raise `TypeError`. This can break assignee outbound sync for those integrations on every task, not just the new inbound source path. All concrete overrides need to be updated or call sites made backward-compatible.

Source guard suppresses outbound sync for all issues on the same integration

`should_sync` returns `False` whenever `sync_source.integration_id` matches the target integration. The outbound path enumerates every `ExternalIssue` linked to the group (`sync_group_assignee_outbound`), and a group can be linked to multiple issues in the same integration or across org integrations. An inbound assignment from one external issue will therefore skip outbound assignment to every other linked issue in that integration, not just the originating issue; those linked issue trackers silently remain out of sync. The source should carry a more specific identifier (for example, org integration id and external issue id) and the guard should compare narrowly.

true_positives.golden_comment: MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains pass, failing to implement its required abstract methods: counter_names (property), get_dedupe_value(), get_group_key_values(), and build_occurrence_and_event_data(). This will cause a TypeError at runtime when the class is instantiated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
MetricAlertDetectorHandler is abstract and cannot be instantiated

StatefulDetectorHandler declares abstract methods such as counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and the new build_occurrence_and_event_data. MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits it with only `pass` and implements none of them, so Python treats it as an abstract class. MetricAlertFire.detector_handler is set to this class, and Detector.detector_handler does `group_type.detector_handler(self)`; for a detector of this type, that will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler ...`. Implement the required methods or keep this handler as a concrete non-stateful stub that returns an empty dict.

true_positives.golden_comment: Docstring says this returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but the method now returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. Consider updating the docstring to match the new return type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
evaluate docstring still says it returns a list

The docstring for `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` says it returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`, but the method now returns `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`. This can mislead implementers and callers about the contract.

true_positives.golden_comment: Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Expected occurrences are built with wrong evaluated values

In `test_state_results_multi_group`, `group_2` is evaluated with value 10 from the data packet, but the expected occurrence is built with value 6. The mock `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` currently ignores `value`, so the test passes and does not verify that the hook receives the actual group value. Similar mismatches occur in `test_results_on_change` (evaluates 100, expects 6) and `test_dedupe` (evaluates 8, expects 6). Use the same value as the evaluation so the hook's value argument is covered.

false_positives.candidate:
Expected occurrence built with the wrong group key in TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe

`build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "val1", 6, ...)` creates an occurrence whose fingerprint is `[<detector_id>:val1]`, but the evaluated call uses `expected_result.group_key`, which is `"group_key"` (and value 10). The actual result's occurrence will have fingerprint `[<detector_id>:group_key]`. Since IssueOccurrence is a dataclass and equality includes fingerprint, the assertion comparing the handler result to `expected_result` will fail. Build the expected occurrence with the same group_key/value that will be evaluated.

Occurrence produced before detector state is committed; retries can duplicate issues

`process_detectors` calls `create_issue_occurrence_from_result` for each result and only afterwards calls `handler.commit_state_updates()` (line 68). If the process crashes or the DB/Redis state commit fails after Kafka production, the dedupe/status state is not advanced. A retry of the same data packet will evaluate the same transition again and emit another occurrence/status change. This is now a real path because stateful detectors return non-None occurrence results. Commit state before producing, or make occurrence production idempotent/transactional.

true_positives.golden_comment: The function modifies the config variable to include display values but then returns the original monitor.config instead of the modified version.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
get_monitor_environment_context returns the unmodified config, discarding schedule_type display value

The function creates `config = monitor_environment.monitor.config.copy()` and conditionally replaces `config["schedule_type"]` with `get_schedule_type_display()`, but the returned dict uses `"config": monitor_environment.monitor.config` instead of the modified `config`. The copy and mutation are therefore dead, and issue occurrence contexts will contain the raw `schedule_type` choice/enum value rather than the human-readable display value. This defeats the only reason for making the copy and gives consumers incorrect monitor config data.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The code fetches MonitorCheckIn objects by ID when the required data already exists in previous_checkins. This creates an unnecessary database query.

false_positives.candidate:
Moved module-level symbols removed from mark_failed without re-export

This refactor removes `SimpleCheckIn`, `mark_failed_threshold`, `create_issue_platform_occurrence`, `get_failure_reason`, and `get_monitor_environment_context` from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` and moves them to other modules without leaving backwards-compatible re-exports in `mark_failed.py`. Any existing code or tests that import these names from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` will now fail with ImportError. All importers should be updated, or the old module should re-export the moved names.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Spawned flusher processes are not killed before replacement

`self.mp_context` is `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")`, so the entries in `self.processes` are `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess` objects. The top-level `multiprocessing.Process` is a different class on systems where the default context is not spawn, so `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` can be false for these spawned processes. In `_ensure_processes_alive`, a hung process is therefore not killed, but `_create_process_for_shards` still starts a replacement for the same shards. This leaves the old flusher alive and can cause two processes to flush/produce the same segments concurrently, leading to duplicate spans in Kafka. The same incorrect check in `join()` (line 346) also prevents spawned processes from being terminated on timeout. Check against `self.mp_context.Process` or `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() skips termination of remaining processes once timeout expires

In `join`, the loop checks `remaining_time <= 0` and then `break`s out of the entire process loop. If `next_step.join(timeout)` or waiting for an earlier flusher process consumes the whole deadline, later flusher processes are never waited on and never reach `process.terminate()`. Because `stopped` only requests a graceful shutdown, a stuck child can keep running after `join()` returns, leaking resources or continuing to produce during shutdown/rebalance. The loop should still terminate all remaining processes after the deadline expires, or calculate per-process timeouts differently.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

false_positives.candidate:
Multi-process flusher test only checks process mapping, not flushing behavior

`test_flusher_processes_limit` verifies that `SpanFlusher` creates the expected number of processes and distributes shards, but it never submits spans, polls the pipeline, or asserts produced Kafka payloads. The actual behavior of multiple flusher processes sharing shards—flushing segments from Redis, producing to Kafka, and completing `done_flush_segments`—is not exercised, so a regression in the multiprocess flushing path would not be caught by this test. Add a functional test with spans on multiple partitions and assert the produced messages.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
OffsetTracker can commit past an offset gap after the prior offset is committed

In get_committable_offsets, start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset) treats every offset below min_offset as already accounted for. If a gap exists before min_offset, it is forgotten after the first commit because mark_committed removes all offsets <= the committed offset from all_offsets. For example, with completed offsets 100, 102, and 103, the first call commits 100 and removes it; the next call sees min_offset=102 and last_committed=100, so start=102, and it returns 103, committing past missing offset 101. This violates the class's gap-handling contract and can cause Kafka offsets to be skipped if such a gap ever occurs.

Shutdown exits workers before queued items are drained

FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown = True while work is still queued, then calls q.shutdown(immediate=False) and joins. OrderedQueueWorker.run checks self.shutdown at the top of its loop, so a worker that is between items exits immediately without draining queued WorkItems. A worker blocked on get() may also not be woken by Queue.shutdown(immediate=False), causing join(timeout=5.0) to return while the daemon thread remains blocked. The result is queued messages not processed on shutdown and leaked worker threads; those offsets will be reprocessed after restart, causing duplicate work.

Unbounded queues provide no backpressure

Each work_queue is created as queue.Queue() with no maxsize. Since submit never blocks, a slow group or worker can accumulate an unbounded number of queued WorkItems and offset-tracking entries. The class docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but these queues never fill. Under sustained slowdown this can exhaust memory and take down the consumer instead of slowing Kafka consumption.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key uses raw underscore concatenation and can collide

`userPermDenialCacheKey` builds the cache key as `namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent`. Because the fields are not length-prefixed or escaped, different tuples containing underscores can map to the same key; for example, `name="a", parent="b_c"` and `name="a_b", parent="c"` both produce a suffix of `a_b_c`. A cached denial for one dashboard/folder can then falsely deny access to a different allowed resource for the same user/action until the TTL expires. Use a collision-resistant key such as a hash of the fields or length-delimited concatenation.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

false_positives.candidate:
Check re-queries permissions for every distinct denied resource

After a cached permission map is found but the requested resource is not allowed, `Check` unconditionally falls through to `getIdentityPermissions`, which queries the permission store. The subsequent denial cache only prevents repeats for the exact `name`+`parent` tuple. For a user with a cached empty or stale permission map, each unique `Name` causes a fresh DB permissions query. This allows sequential requests with arbitrary unique resource names to bypass the action-level permission cache and impose significant DB load. Consider rate-limiting or deduplicating these fallbacks, or using a per-action last-refresh/negative TTL instead of a full DB query per denied resource.

Remote AuthZ client still caches decisions and bypasses the server-side fix

`newRemoteRBACClient` still configures `authzlib.NewClient` with a 30-second local cache. The PR disables the authlib client cache only for the in-process path via `NoopCache`. In remote/standalone deployments, `Check`/`List` results, including false denials, can be served from this client-side cache and never reach the server-side denial-cache and DB requery logic. Users in those modes can therefore still be denied access to newly created dashboards/folders for up to 30 seconds. If the fix is intended for all modes, the remote client cache needs to be disabled, shortened, or invalidated on resource creation.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing React key on GrafanaRuleListItem in FilterView

In `rules.map`, the computed `key` is passed to `DataSourceRuleLoader` and `UnknownRuleListItem`, but the Grafana branch renders `<GrafanaRuleListItem>` without `key={key}`. React falls back to index keys, so list items can be reconciled incorrectly when rules are appended, reordered, or filtered, and React will emit a key warning.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence menu item is shown in ruler-less list view but the drawer is never rendered

`AlertRuleMenu` can show the Silence notifications item based on the new Prom-based `canSilence` ability, and clicking it calls `setShowSilenceDrawer(true)`. But `RuleActionsButtons` only renders `<SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer>` when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true. In the new list path `rule` (the ruler rule) is undefined, so the drawer is never rendered. The user sees and can click Silence, but nothing happens.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete and pause actions are still gated on rulerRule, so they disappear in the ruler-less list view

The new `GrafanaRuleListItem` renders `RuleActionsButtons` with only `promRule`, so `AlertRuleMenu` receives `rulerRule` as undefined. However, Delete is still rendered only when `canDelete && rulerRule` (line 165), and Pause is still rendered only when `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` is true (line 123). The component now computes `canDelete` and `canPause` from Prom-based abilities, but users cannot ever see or use those actions in the list view because the old ruler-based guards remain.

Federated rule immutability lost for CombinedRule callers

`useAllAlertRuleAbilities` is now implemented by delegating to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities(rule.rulerRule, groupIdentifierV2)`, but `useAllRulerRuleAbilities` hardcodes `isFederated = false` and has no access to the original rule group. The previous `useAllAlertRuleAbilities` checked `isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)`, which made update and delete abilities unsupported for federated rule groups. As a result, callers using `useAlertRuleAbility`/`useAlertRuleAbilities` with a `CombinedRule` will now treat federated data-source rule groups as mutable, allowing edit/delete actions to be shown and invoked when they should be blocked.

skipToken path still evaluates Grafana permissions and can allow Duplicate for cloud rules

`useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` maps `skipToken` to `undefined` and calls `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined)`. For a missing rule, `useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable` returns `loading: false`, so `MaybeSupported` becomes `AlwaysSupported` and `duplicateSupported` becomes true. The hook then evaluates `getRulesPermissions('grafana')`. In `AlertRuleMenu`, this hook is called with `skipToken` for non-Grafana (cloud) Prom rules, so a user with Grafana rule-create permission but without the data source's create permission can see Duplicate enabled for a cloud rule even though the ruler-based ability would deny it.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Interpolation makes `isQueryWithRangeVariable` guard ineffective

`runSplitQuery` now maps targets through `datasource.applyTemplateVariables` before `partition(queries, (query) => !querySupportsSplitting(query))`. `querySupportsSplitting` calls `isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr)` to avoid splitting queries containing `$__range` (or similar range variables), but after interpolation those variables have already been replaced with duration literals, so the guard no longer detects them. Queries that were deliberately excluded from time-splitting will now be split, and each subrequest will use an expression interpolated against the full request range rather than the intended unsplit query. This can produce incorrect result semantics. The check should be done against the pre-interpolation expression, or the guard must be intentionally re-evaluated with tests.

Shard splitting applies template variables twice

`runShardSplitQuery` now applies `applyTemplateVariables` to every target at line 52. Later, `splitQueriesByStreamShard` passes those same targets to `runSplitQuery` (line 163), and the modified `runSplitQuery` applies `applyTemplateVariables` again to its targets (querySplitting.ts line 299). This double interpolation is not guaranteed to be idempotent; in particular, if `request.filters` contains ad hoc filters, `applyTemplateVariables` can insert those filters into the expression on each call, duplicating filter selectors in the final query. The new test expectation that `applyTemplateVariables` is called five times for one target reflects this duplication rather than guarding against it. `runSplitQuery` should support skipping interpolation when the caller has already interpolated, or this path should avoid pre-interpolating before delegating.

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Plugin request logs no longer include traceID

The previous logRequest appended `traceID` from `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)` to the `Plugin Request Completed` log params. This change removes that field entirely, and the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware only adds endpoint, pluginId, dsName/dsUID, and uname. As a result these plugin request logs lose trace correlation, which is a regression for debugging and tracing. Add `traceID` to `logParams` (or to `instrumentContext`) before logging.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, hiding logs made via FromContext

LoggerMiddleware now logs through `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`. A TestLogger passed to NewLoggerMiddleware will have `FromContext` return a brand-new TestLogger, so the original TestLogger's `InfoLogs` (and other log fields) will not be incremented. Any existing or future logger middleware test using this fake cannot observe the log call. Return `f` (or otherwise share the log fields) so FromContext preserves observability.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

false_positives.candidate:
Logger name still says 'plugin.instrumentation'

After renaming InstrumentationMiddleware to MetricsMiddleware and adding ContextualLoggerMiddleware, the logger for LoggerMiddleware is still constructed with `log.New("plugin.instrumentation")`. Log messages emitted by the request logger will continue to appear under the old instrumentation name, which is misleading and inconsistent with the PR's naming goal. Rename it to reflect the actual logger purpose (for example `plugin.requests` or `plugin.logger`).

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Count-then-insert race can exceed anonymous device limit

`CreateOrUpdateDevice` performs a `CountDevices` check and then inserts when below limit without any transaction, lock, or serializable isolation. Concurrent anonymous sign-ins with different device IDs can all observe a count below `deviceLimit` and then insert, exceeding the configured limit. If the limit is intended to be enforced, the count and insert/update must be made atomic.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Rejected devices are cached before persistence, allowing device-limit bypass

`tagDeviceUI` checks and sets the local cache before `CreateOrUpdateDevice`. When a new device ID hits the limit, `CreateOrUpdateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, but the device ID is already cached. A retry with the same `X-Grafana-Device-Id` finds the cache entry, skips the device store and limit check, returns nil, and `Anonymous.Authenticate` completes successfully. This makes the configured limit trivially bypassable. Move the cache write to after a successful DB write or invalidate the key on error.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
New updateDevice SQL uses `?` placeholders on PostgreSQL

The new `updateDevice` query uses `?` placeholders unconditionally (`... WHERE device_id = ? ...`), but PostgreSQL requires `$1`-style placeholders. The same file's `CreateOrUpdateDevice` explicitly uses `$1` for `migrator.Postgres`, so this path will fail when `device_limit` is reached on Postgres. Because `Anonymous.Authenticate` only treats `ErrDeviceLimitReached` as fatal and logs other TagDevice errors, a placeholder error here is swallowed and the device limit is not enforced.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Normal cleanup batches logged as errors with full ID lists

The new cleanup paths call `r.log.Error` for successful fetch/delete iterations (`Annotations to clean by time`, `cleaned annotations by time`, etc.). The fetch log returns before logging when `fetchIDs` fails, so those logs always have err == nil and represent normal operation. This generates error-level noise/false alerts and logs the full `ids` slice per batch, which is very large for big `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` values. Use debug or info level and avoid dumping all IDs (same pattern at lines 537, 554, 557, 576 and 579).

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute

This change is unrelated to the annotation deadlock fix and makes the entire cleanup suite (old annotations, expired snapshots/dashboard versions/images, temp users, short URLs, query history) run 10x more often. `clean` has a 9-minute timeout, so with a 1-minute ticker a long cleanup can finish and then immediately consume a queued tick, creating sustained high DB/CPU load. More frequent annotation cleanup may also reintroduce the write/lock pressure that the PR is trying to avoid. This appears accidental; revert or explain and justify this scheduling change.

false_positives.candidate:
Non-SQLite deletion path can exceed database bind limits

`deleteByIDs` builds `id IN (?,?,...)` with one placeholder per ID for every non-SQLite database. The previous subquery-based DELETE did not bind one parameter per row, so very large `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` values were safer. PostgreSQL has a bind-parameter limit of 32767, and MySQL/similar databases have practical packet/query-size limits. If the configured batch size exceeds the database limit, cleanup fails even though the old statement worked. The SQLite branch is special-cased by inlining IDs; the non-SQLite path should also chunk the delete by IDs or otherwise use a dialect-safe limit.

Per-subtest cleanup is registered after data is inserted

Each table-driven subtest calls `createTestAnnotations` and performs initial count assertions before registering the `t.Cleanup` that deletes `annotation` and `annotation_tag`. If setup or one of these initial `require` assertions fails, `t.Cleanup` is never registered, leaving up to 40k annotations and 80k tags in the shared test DB; subsequent subtests then run against polluted data and produce cascading failures. Register the cleanup before inserting/asserting data, or otherwise guarantee cleanup runs on any setup failure.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Legacy DeleteCollection result is recorded as a storage duration

In `DeleteCollection`'s legacy goroutine, `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ..., startLegacy)` uses the storage metric for the legacy call and starts from `startLegacy`. This mislabels legacy duration/errors as unified-storage operations and leaves the legacy metric unpopulated. It should call `d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete success records the object name in the `kind` metric label

After a successful `Storage.Delete`, the code calls `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`, passing `name` where every other call passes `options.Kind`. The `kind` label will contain per-object names instead of the resource kind, producing unbounded metric cardinality and destroying aggregation by kind. It should pass `options.Kind`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are canceled after the handler returns

`Create` starts a goroutine that derives from the caller's `ctx` (`context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`). The same pattern is used in `Delete` (line 110), `Update` (line 135), and `DeleteCollection` (line 163). In the apiserver this `ctx` is the HTTP request context, which is canceled when `ServeHTTP` returns; the dual writer returns immediately after starting the goroutine, so the legacy write races with cancellation and can be canceled before it has completed. Since the legacy write is the safety mechanism for Mode 3, this can silently lose the backup write. Use a request-detached context such as `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` plus an explicit timeout, or a server-owned background context.

Legacy Update recomputes the update instead of writing the object returned by unified storage

`d.Legacy.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, ...)` passes the original `rest.UpdatedObjectInfo` to legacy storage. `UpdatedObjectInfo` is called again by legacy storage against the legacy old object, so it can produce a different object than `res` returned by `d.Storage.Update`, especially when legacy and unified storage are at different versions. The previous implementation wrapped the already-returned unified object (`updateWrapper{updated: obj}`), ensuring legacy wrote the same object. Reinstate that behavior by passing a wrapper that returns `res`; otherwise the legacy backup may be inconsistent with unified storage or fail update validation.

Mode3 integration tests reuse synchronous CRUD assertions and race with legacy writeback

The new Mode3 cases call `doPlaylistTests`, which checks the legacy API immediately after k8s create/update/delete (for example `client.Resource.Create` followed by a legacy `/api/playlists` GET, and `client.Resource.Delete` followed by a legacy GET). With Mode3 those legacy writes are asynchronous, so the test assertions are timing-dependent and can fail intermittently if the goroutine has not completed. Mode3 needs a poll/wait mechanism for the legacy side or a separate test suite that accounts for asynchronous propagation.

Mode3 unit tests never wait for or assert the asynchronous legacy write

The success tests configure legacy mock expectations (for example, `setupLegacyFn` in `TestMode3_Create`) but return immediately after the synchronous unified-storage call. Because the actual legacy write happens in a goroutine, the test passes even if the legacy mock is never called, and no `m.AssertExpectations` or synchronization verifies it. This makes the core Mode3 behavior (legacy backup write) untested and can also leave background goroutines running after the subtest exits. Add a wait group or injectable async executor and assert the legacy calls.

Storage Create failure is recorded as a legacy duration

On `d.Storage.Create` error, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` using `startStorage`. This increments the legacy error/duration metric for an operation in which legacy was never called, while the unified-storage error is not recorded as a storage duration. It should call `d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. The same mistake exists in `Update` at line 129.

Unordered goroutines can leave stale data in legacy storage

Each successful storage write launches an independent goroutine for the legacy write, with no per-object queue, mutex, version check, or ordering guarantee. Two concurrent updates or deletes for the same object can complete in unified storage in one order but be applied to legacy in the opposite order due to goroutine scheduling. For example, an older `Update` goroutine can run after a newer one, leaving legacy with the older object even though unified storage has the newer one. A per-key worker, resourceVersion precondition, or other ordered writeback mechanism is needed to ensure the legacy backup does not regress.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
GetWebAssets does not re-check the cache after acquiring the write lock

The fast path reads entryPointAssetsCache under RLock, but once it sees nil it releases and later calls Lock without re-reading the cache. Multiple goroutines that observed nil before the first writer populated the cache will all enter the slow path serially, each opening and parsing the manifest while holding the exclusive lock. If one of those later reloads fails, it can overwrite an already-valid cache with nil, causing subsequent requests to retry and potentially fail. After acquiring Lock, the function should re-check entryPointAssetsCache (and return it when cfg.Env != setting.Dev) before doing any I/O.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
GetWebAssets does not re-check the cache after acquiring the write lock

The fast path reads entryPointAssetsCache under RLock, but once it sees nil it releases and later calls Lock without re-reading the cache. Multiple goroutines that observed nil before the first writer populated the cache will all enter the slow path serially, each opening and parsing the manifest while holding the exclusive lock. If one of those later reloads fails, it can overwrite an already-valid cache with nil, causing subsequent requests to retry and potentially fail. After acquiring Lock, the function should re-check entryPointAssetsCache (and return it when cfg.Env != setting.Dev) before doing any I/O.

false_positives.candidate:
No concurrent regression test for the data race fix

This change adds synchronization to GetWebAssets but no test exercises concurrent calls. A race-enabled test that calls GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines and accesses the returned assets would help detect a regression back to unsynchronized access of the global entryPointAssetsCache.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions always returns false, making the SQL feature flag dead

The helper initializes `enabled` to the negation of `h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions)`, then returns false both when `enabled` is true and when it is false. As a result, every QueryTypeSQL is rejected before parsing regardless of whether the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle is on. If the toggle is meant to control the feature, this should return `h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(...)`; if the feature is intentionally unconditional-off, the function should just return false and not consult the toggle. The current code leaves a contradictory, dead toggle.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

false_positives.candidate:
No automated tests cover the SQL-expression disabling

This security fix adds a hard rejection for QueryTypeSQL and replaces DuckDB with stubs, but no tests are included. There is no check that ReadQuery rejects SQL expressions with the intended error, that NewSQLCommand and sql.TablesList return not-implemented errors, or that the feature flag behavior is as intended. A future regression could remove or invert this guard without CI noticing.

Original DuckDB json_serialize_sql command construction is still present

TablesList still interpolates user SQL into `SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s')` after only replacing single quotes and passes it to RunCommands. The new stub RunCommands returns not implemented so the command is not executed today, but the DuckDB-specific parsing path that carried the original RCE/LFI vector remains wired into NewSQLCommand. Any future real DB implementation or alternate caller would re-enable the vulnerable path. The fix would be safer if this serialization logic were removed rather than only stubbed.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BuildIndex scoped lock allows concurrent builds for the same key

The lock was moved from the entire BuildIndex path to only the final cache insertion. However searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex has no per-key synchronization: two callers that both see GetIndex return nil for the same NamespacedResource can now run BuildIndex concurrently. For file-backed indexes this means two calls to bleve.New on the same directory can open/modify the same bleve data files concurrently, causing corruption or an error; for memory indexes one built index is leaked and the cache is last-writer-wins. Use a per-key lock/singleflight or re-check the cache after acquiring the lock.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
Eager Init failure returns without cleaning up partial startup

NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) before returning the server. If Init fails, it returns nil and discards s, but Init can have partially succeeded: lifecycle.Init may have opened the backend, and search.init may have already started its watcher goroutine before a later step such as initWatcher fails. Since no server is returned, the caller cannot call Stop, and s.cancel/lifecycle.Stop are not invoked on this error path, leaking the DB lifecycle and background watchers. On Init failure, cancel s.ctx and stop the lifecycle if it was initialized before returning.

Postgres storage server integration test is skipped

This PR adds a skip for the postgres backend in TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer, with a TODO to fix the test later. Since the PR changes unified storage initialization from lazy to eager, postgres coverage for this startup path is removed exactly when it is most likely to catch startup or indexing regressions. Fix the test or ensure equivalent postgres coverage runs in CI.

Resource version returned by build is discarded so watch events can be lost

s.build returns the last resource version read while listing that namespace, specifically so a watch can resume after it. searchSupport.init discards that value with `_`. After all indexes are built it calls WatchWriteEvents, which in the SQL backend starts from the latest RV at that moment. Any write that lands after a namespace was listed but before WatchWriteEvents captures the baseline becomes the baseline itself and is never emitted to the search index, leaving the search index missing that update until a later event or rebuild. Keep the per-resource RV and pass it to the watcher, or start watching before the build and buffer events.

Search init worker goroutines race on shared variables

Inside searchSupport.init the errgroup workers are limited but still concurrent. Each goroutine executes `totalBatchesIndexed++` and `_, _, err = s.build(...)` on variables shared with all other workers. These are unsynchronized writes to the same memory, so this is a data race. The `err` capture is also semantically wrong: one goroutine can overwrite the outer `err` before another returns it, causing a build failure to be reported as success or vice versa. Declare `err` locally with `:=` in the closure and use an atomic counter for totalBatchesIndexed.

Search watch goroutine panics on closed event channel

The goroutine started in searchSupport.init reads from the write-events channel with `v := <-events` and immediately calls `s.handleEvent(watchctx, v)` without checking the channel-open boolean. The SQL watcher closes its stream when the backend stops (`defer close(stream)` in the poller), after which a receive returns a nil *WrittenEvent. `handleEvent` dereferences `evt.Type`, causing a nil-pointer panic that can crash the process during shutdown. Check `v, ok := <-events` and return on `!ok`, and wire the loop to a cancellable context.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test cleanup registers the literal alias "alias" instead of the created provider alias

In testCacheIDPForLogin, the cleanup for each newly created identity provider is registered as testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove, using the literal string "alias" rather than the variable alias such as "idp-alias-" + i or "idp-alias-20". The same mistake is repeated at line 425. Therefore the actual created providers are not removed after the test, and cleanup may attempt to delete a nonexistent/wrong provider. Use the actual alias variable or the created provider resource in addCleanup.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
getForLogin can return identity providers that are not available for login

The new getForLogin cache stores only internal IDs and, on both cache miss and cache hit, reconstructs the result by calling session.identityProviders().getById(id) and adding every non-null model to the returned stream without applying IdentityProviderStorageProvider.LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate(). The delegate search can include organization-linked IDPs whose organization is disabled, because it filters on BROKER_PUBLIC and ORGANIZATION_ID but does not evaluate the organization's enabled state. createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel then intentionally makes isEnabled() false for such IDPs. As a result, getForLogin violates its contract by returning IDPs that are not available for login. The OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean had to add extra isEnabled() filters, but other callers will still receive disabled brokers. Filter the final stream with getLoginPredicate() or otherwise invalidate/refresh the login cache when organization enabled state changes.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default KeyStore provider, not BouncyCastle

KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider() returns the JCA provider backing the default keystore type (usually SUN/SunJCE on a stock JDK), not a BouncyCastle provider. Callers of CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() may check for null or use the returned provider to request BC-specific algorithms, so this can lead to NoSuchAlgorithmException or use of an unintended security provider. If this provider intentionally does not use BouncyCastle, it should return null or a provider that actually supplies the algorithms it claims to support, and callers must handle that.

true_positives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Indefinite BER length leaks into DER parser and causes unchecked exception

readLength() returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding (0x80). readInteger() then passes that -1 to read(int), which executes new byte[length] and throws unchecked NegativeArraySizeException rather than the declared IOException. A malformed DER signature can therefore bypass normal error handling. This DER decoder should reject indefinite-length encoding explicitly, and readInteger() should also reject an empty INTEGER before new BigInteger(bytes) to avoid NumberFormatException.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract order() method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

Adding an abstract order() method to the public CryptoProvider interface is binary and source incompatible for any external implementation compiled against an older Keycloak version. During CryptoIntegration.detectProvider, sorting calls order() on every loaded provider, so an older implementation will fail with AbstractMethodError even if it is the only provider on the classpath. Provide a default implementation such as default int order() { return 0; } or preserve SPI compatibility.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.

false_positives.candidate:
Providers with equal order are selected silently and arbitrarily

The new logic replaces the previous fail-fast multiple-provider check with sorting by order(). But all built-in providers except AuthzClientCryptoProvider (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider) return 200. If two of them end up on the classpath, the selection depends on ServiceLoader encounter order and no error is raised. This can silently select the non-FIPS provider in a FIPS-required environment, or vice versa, defeating the old classpath integrity guard. Distinct orders are needed for each real provider, or a tie at the top order should still fail.

Test does not verify the first DER-to-raw conversion against the original signature

The test computes rsConcat from the JCA DER signature, converts it back to asn1Des, then only asserts that converting asn1Des back to raw gives the same rsConcat. A paired defect in asn1derToConcatenatedRS and concatenatedRSToASN1DER could pass this roundtrip while still producing the wrong raw signature from the original DER, or the wrong DER from the raw signature. It should also assert that asn1Des equals the original sign, or compare against known DER/raw vectors.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission returns the synthetic all-clients resource name

getClientsWithPermission iterates all resources of type CLIENTS, including the all-clients resource whose name is AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE ("Clients"). If a policy grants the requested scope on that all-resource, hasGrantedPermission returns true and the code adds resource.getName(), i.e. "Clients", to the returned set. Callers expect this set to contain concrete client IDs, so the all-resource grant is not expanded into actual clients and a nonexistent client ID is returned. The all-resource should be skipped or expanded to the corresponding concrete client IDs.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Per-client permission check can dereference a null all-clients resource

In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission(ClientModel, String), AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...) may return null when the all-resource for the Clients type does not exist. The code then immediately calls authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource) without a null check, causing a NullPointerException. This is especially likely for an existing admin permissions client that was not upgraded with the new schema. The method should handle resource == null by returning false or ensuring initialization first.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
Existing admin permission clients are not upgraded with the new Clients resource type and scopes

AdminPermissionsSchema.init() returns early whenever realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is already non-null, so realms that already had the admin permissions client created under the previous V2 schema will not get the newly added Clients resource type or its scopes (configure, map-roles-client-scope, map-roles-composite). Later, client permission creation can fail with ModelException "No scopes found." and client permission evaluation can fail or NPE because the all-Clients resource is missing. The init method needs to be idempotent and add missing schema entries for existing admin permission clients.

Void require methods are documented as returning boolean

The Javadoc for requireView() and requireViewClientScopes() says "Returns true if ... returns true", but both methods are void and throw ForbiddenException when the corresponding check fails. This misdocuments the API and should say that it throws ForbiddenException when the check returns false.

getResourceName does not resolve Clients resources

AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceName has special handling for the USERS resource type but not for the newly added CLIENTS resource type. For client permissions/resources it falls through to resource.getDisplayName(), but client resources created by getOrCreateResource use the client's internal id as the resource name and do not set a meaningful display name. Resource name resolution or representation output for client permissions can therefore be null or an internal UUID instead of the client's clientId. A CLIENTS branch should resolve the client and return client.getClientId() or another appropriate display value.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:
Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

false_positives.candidate:
Exit code 3 is reserved by Picocli for execution errors

This change sets RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE to 3 while the preceding comment explicitly refers to picocli.CommandLine.ExitCode. In that interface, 3 is EXECUTION_ERROR. A normal incompatibility result (recreate required) would therefore be indistinguishable from an execution failure if Picocli or any handler returns the standard EXECUTION_ERROR code. The documented contract reserves 1 for unexpected errors, so use a non-picocli-reserved code for recreate (e.g. keep 4 for recreate and move feature-disabled to another value such as 5).

Exit-code contract is not asserted by the new tests

testFeatureNotEnabled only asserts the stderr message and does not assert that the process exits with CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED (4). Likewise, testWrongVersions checks the error messages for incompatible Keycloak/Infinispan versions but never asserts exit code 3, even though this PR changes the recreate exit code from 4 to 3 and documents it. Since exit codes are the scripting contract for this tool, the tests should assert them to prevent regressions such as the code returning the old exit code while the docs show the new one.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
VIEW permission on all groups grants manage rights to all groups

canManage() checks hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE). A caller who only has the global Groups view scope is therefore treated as having manage rights. requireManage() is used by GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup() and group update/delete flows, so this allows users with view-only permission to create or modify groups. The check should require AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE only.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns authorization resource IDs instead of group model IDs and may not enumerate per-group resources

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() iterates resources returned by findByType and passes groupResource.getId() to hasPermission(), then adds that ID to the returned set. The returned set is used as GroupModel IDs for the UserModel.GROUPS search attribute in UsersResource and BruteForceUsersResource. However, group permission resources are created by AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource() with the group model ID as the resource name and a separate generated authorization resource UUID as the resource ID; getId() is not the group ID. In addition, those per-group resources are not created with type Groups, so findByType may not find them. The result is that user search/count filtering by viewable groups receives invalid or empty group IDs and can return wrong results. The code should use groupResource.getName() and ensure resources are actually typed and enumerable.

false_positives.candidate:
Existing admin permissions clients are not migrated with the new Groups resource type and scopes

init() returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is already non-null. Realms that already initialized the V2 admin permissions schema before this change will therefore not get the new Groups resource type or the new group scopes. Later, GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission() can call getResourceTypeResource(session, server, GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE), receive null, and then call policyStore.findByResource(server, resource), causing an NPE; alternatively, Groups permissions cannot be configured or enforced for those realms. Initialization should create the missing Groups resource/scopes for existing admin permission clients.

true_positives.golden_comment: The translation is in Italian instead of Lithuanian. This should be translated to Lithuanian to match the file's locale (messages_lt.properties).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Lithuanian account message `totpStep1` is now Italian

The new value is "Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:", which is Italian. Lithuanian users will see Italian text in the account authenticator setup. The text should be translated into Lithuanian.

true_positives.golden_comment: The totpStep1 value uses Traditional Chinese terms in the Simplified Chinese file (zh_CN), which is likely incorrect for this locale. Please verify the locale‑appropriate translation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Simplified Chinese file contains Traditional Chinese text

`totpStep1=在您的手機上安裝以下應用程式之一：` uses Traditional Chinese characters (`手機`, `應用程式`) in the zh_CN Simplified Chinese resource. Simplified Chinese users will see mixed-script text. It should be written in Simplified Chinese, e.g. `在您的手机上安装以下应用之一：`.

The method name 'santizeAnchors' should be 'sanitizeAnchors' (missing 'i').

false_positives.candidate:
Account UI message switched from i18next to Java MessageFormat/ChoiceFormat syntax

This file uses i18next `{{0}}` interpolation throughout, but the new `error-invalid-multivalued-size` value uses Java MessageFormat `{0}`, `{1}`, and `{2,choice,...}`. Search init worker goroutines race on shared variables

Inside searchSupport.init the errgroup workers are limited but still concurrent. Each goroutine executes `totalBatchesIndexed++` and `_, _, err = s.build(...)` on variables shared with all other workers. These are unsynchronized writes to the same memory, so this is a data race. The `err` capture is also semantically wrong: one goroutine can overwrite the outer `err` before another returns it, causing a build failure to be reported as success or vice versa. Declare `err` locally with `:=` in the closure and use an atomic counter for totalBatchesIndexed.

Search watch goroutine panics on closed event channel

The goroutine started in searchSupport.init reads from the write-events channel with `v := <-events` and immediately calls `s.handleEvent(watchctx, v)` without checking the channel-open boolean. The SQL watcher closes its stream when the backend stops (`defer close(stream)` in the poller), after which a receive returns a nil *WrittenEvent. `handleEvent` dereferences `evt.Type`, causing a nil-pointer panic that can crash the process during shutdown. Check `v, ok := <-events` and return on `!ok`, and wire the loop to a cancellable context.

Resource version returned by build is discarded so watch events can be lost

s.build returns the last resource version read while listing that namespace, specifically so a watch can resume after it. searchSupport.init discards that value with `_`. After all indexes are built it calls WatchWriteEvents, which in the SQL backend starts from the latest RV at that moment. Any write that lands after a namespace was listed but before WatchWriteEvents captures the baseline becomes the baseline itself and is never emitted to the search index, leaving the search index missing that update until a later event or rebuild. Keep the per-resource RV and pass it to the watcher, or start watching before the build and buffer events.

Since the PR changes unified storage initialization from lazy to eager, postgres coverage for this startup path is removed exactly when it is most likely to catch startup or indexing regressions. NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) before returning the server. If Init fails, it returns nil and discards s, but Init can have partially succeeded: lifecycle.Init may have opened the backend, and search.init may have already started its watcher goroutine before a later step such as initWatcher fails. Since no server is returned, the caller cannot call Stop, and s.cancel/lifecycle.Stop are not invoked on this error path, leaking the DB lifecycle and background watchers. false_positives.candidate:
OffsetTracker can commit past an offset gap after the prior offset is committed

In get_committable_offsets, start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset) treats every offset below min_offset as already accounted for. If a gap exists before min_offset, it is forgotten after the first commit because mark_committed removes all offsets <= the committed offset from all_offsets. For example, with completed offsets 100, 102, and 103, the first call commits 100 and removes it; the next call sees min_offset=102 and last_committed=100, so start=102, and it returns 103, committing past missing offset 101. This violates the class's gap-handling contract and can cause Kafka offsets to be skipped if such a gap ever occurs.

Unbounded queues provide no backpressure

Each work_queue is created as queue.Queue() with no maxsize. Since submit never blocks, a slow group or worker can accumulate an unbounded number of queued WorkItems and offset-tracking entries. The class docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but these queues never fill. Under sustained slowdown this can exhaust memory and take down the consumer instead of slowing Kafka consumption.

Shutdown exits workers before queued items are drained

FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown = True while work is still queued, then calls q.shutdown(immediate=False) and joins. OrderedQueueWorker.run checks self.shutdown at the top of its loop, so a worker that is between items exits immediately without draining queued WorkItems. A worker blocked on get() may also not be woken by Queue.shutdown(immediate=False), causing join(timeout=5.0) to return while the daemon thread remains blocked. The result is queued messages not processed on shutdown and leaked worker threads; those offsets will be reprocessed after restart, causing duplicate work.

false_positives.candidate:
Eviction can remove the root/segment span from a segment

The script trims the sorted set to 1000 members with `zpopmin(set_key, span_count - 1000)`. `zpopmin` removes members with the smallest `end_timestamp_precise` scores and makes no exception for the segment root span. A root span can have one of the smallest end timestamps, for example when async child spans outlive the root span or multiple spans share the same timestamp. The current root span can also be inserted and immediately popped in the same script call. If the root span is dropped, the buffered segment is later flushed without its root span, yet the `has_root_span` flag may still be set because it is based on the HRS key or current `is_root_span` and is not cleared when the root payload is removed. Downstream receives a malformed segment whose `segment_id` no longer appears as a span.

ZUNIONSTORE default SUM corrupts scores on duplicate payloads

Both `zunionstore` calls use Redis's default aggregate SUM. If the same payload member already exists in the destination and source, for example when Kafka at-least-once delivery reprocesses the same span, its score is added to itself and `end_timestamp_precise` becomes roughly doubled. The score no longer represents the span's end time, which breaks the eviction order used by `zpopmin` and can cause the wrong spans to be evicted. The operation should be made idempotent for score preservation, such as using `AGGREGATE MIN` or another strategy.

Redirect traversal limit reduced from 10000 to 1000

The script now follows parent redirects only through `i = 0..1000`. If a segment tree has more than 1000 redirect levels, the loop exits without reaching the canonical root, but the script still writes `hset(main_redirect_key, span_id, set_span_id)` using the last intermediate ID. This can join the span to the wrong segment or split a segment that the previous 10000-iteration limit would have handled. If the limit is intentional for performance, the truncation case should be handled explicitly rather than writing a potentially incorrect redirect.

No test covers the new eviction behavior

The new insertion-time eviction logic in `add-buffer.lua` is not covered by tests. Existing buffer tests insert only a handful of spans, so they cannot catch regressions where `zpopmin` drops the root span, evicts the wrong spans, or the hardcoded limit diverges from `max_segment_spans`. A test that inserts more than 1000 spans and asserts the root span is preserved and the segment is capped correctly is needed.

`invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined but no caller is added in this PR. Eligibility is cached for 60 seconds in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`. `upsampled_count` is added to `function_converter` without `private=True`. false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are canceled after the handler returns

`Create` starts a goroutine that derives from the caller's `ctx` (`context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`). The same pattern is used in `Delete` (line 110), `Update` (line 135), and `DeleteCollection` (line 163). In the apiserver this `ctx` is the HTTP request context, which is canceled when `ServeHTTP` returns; the dual writer returns immediately after starting the goroutine, so the legacy write races with cancellation and can be canceled before it has completed. Since the legacy write is the safety mechanism for Mode 3, this can silently lose the backup write. Use a request-detached context such as `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` plus an explicit timeout, or a server-owned background context.

Unordered goroutines can leave stale data in legacy storage

Each successful storage write launches an independent goroutine for the legacy write, with no per-object queue, mutex, version check, or ordering guarantee. Two concurrent updates or deletes for the same object can complete in unified storage in one order but be applied to legacy in the opposite order due to goroutine scheduling. For example, an older `Update` goroutine can run after a newer one, leaving legacy with the older object even though unified storage has the newer one. A per-key worker, resourceVersion precondition, or other ordered writeback mechanism is needed to ensure the legacy backup does not regress.

Legacy Update recomputes the update instead of writing the object returned by unified storage

`d.Legacy.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, ...)` passes the original `rest.UpdatedObjectInfo` to legacy storage. `UpdatedObjectInfo` is called again by legacy storage against the legacy old object, so it can produce a different object than `res` returned by `d.Storage.Update`, especially when legacy and unified storage are at different versions. The previous implementation wrapped the already-returned unified object (`updateWrapper{updated: obj}`), ensuring legacy wrote the same object. Reinstate that behavior by passing a wrapper that returns `res`; otherwise the legacy backup may be inconsistent with unified storage or fail update validation.

Storage Create failure is recorded as a legacy duration

On `d.Storage.Create` error, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` using `startStorage`. This increments the legacy error/duration metric for an operation in which legacy was never called, while the unified-storage error is not recorded as a storage duration. It should call `d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. The same mistake exists in `Update` at line 129.

Mode3 unit tests never wait for or assert the asynchronous legacy write

The success tests configure legacy mock expectations (for example, `setupLegacyFn` in `TestMode3_Create`) but return immediately after the synchronous unified-storage call. Because the actual legacy write happens in a goroutine, the test passes even if the legacy mock is never called, and no `m.AssertExpectations` or synchronization verifies it. This makes the core Mode3 behavior (legacy backup write) untested and can also leave background goroutines running after the subtest exits. Add a wait group or injectable async executor and assert the legacy calls.

Mode3 integration tests reuse synchronous CRUD assertions and race with legacy writeback

The new Mode3 cases call `doPlaylistTests`, which checks the legacy API immediately after k8s create/update/delete (for example `client.Resource.Create` followed by a legacy `/api/playlists` GET, and `client.Resource.Delete` followed by a legacy GET). With Mode3 those legacy writes are asynchronous, so the test assertions are timing-dependent and can fail intermittently if the goroutine has not completed. Mode3 needs a poll/wait mechanism for the legacy side or a separate test suite that accounts for asynchronous propagation.
